frontmatter.name: Bittensor
frontmatter.field: Decentralized incentive / consensus mechanisms for ML networks

What it does.markdown:
Bittensor is a decentralized network in which independent operators ("miners")
run machine-learning models and are paid in the TAO token based on how
useful their outputs are judged to be by other network participants
("validators"). Instead of a central benchmark deciding what's useful, peers
rank each other, and rewards flow from that peer-ranking.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **Subtensor**: the layer-0 blockchain (built on Polkadot Substrate) that
  records peer identity, stake, and the consensus/incentive state.
- **Subnets**: independently defined competitions, each specifying its own
  task (e.g. text generation, image generation) and its own validator
  scoring logic. As of 2026 the network has scaled to roughly 64-128 active
  subnets (sources disagree on the exact figure at time of writing; mainnet
  slot cap is 128, with an expansion to 256 planned). [[FalconX: State of
  Bittensor]](https://www.falconx.io/newsroom/state-of-bittensor-subnet-adoption-trends-network-mechanics-and-covenants-departure)
- **Dynamic TAO (dTAO)**: deployed to mainnet ~Feb 13, 2025. Replaced a
  single global emission pool with per-subnet "alpha" tokens and AMM pools,
  letting TAO holders stake directly into specific subnets rather than the
  network as a whole. [[CryptoBriefing]](https://cryptobriefing.com/bittensor-dynamic-tao-emission-model/)
- **Yuma Consensus (YC)**: the mechanism that turns validator rankings into
  miner payouts (see below).

Built on (foundational lineage).markdown:
**Shapley (1952), "A Value for n-Person Games"** — explicitly cited in
Bittensor's own academic paper, *"Incentivizing Intelligence: The Bittensor
Approach"* (Steeves, Shaabana, Hu, Luus, Liu, Tasker-Steeves et al.), hosted
at [bittensor.com/academia](https://www.bittensor.com/academia), as the
theoretical basis for the peer-ranking mechanism: Shapley values are used to
fairly attribute each peer's contribution to the network's informational
output across permutations of participants.

The whitepaper (*"Bittensor: A Peer-to-Peer Intelligence Market,"* Yuma Rao,
[bittensor.com/whitepaper](https://www.bittensor.com/whitepaper)) separately
cites Fisher Information pruning (LeCun et al. 1989; Yu et al. 2017) as the
theoretical ideal behind how peer-significance weights are ranked, and cites
a cluster of standard deep-learning papers (Hinton et al. 2015 on
distillation/general intelligence, Devlin et al. 2019, Radford et al. 2019,
Shazeer et al. 2017) as background for why peer-to-peer intelligence markets
are plausible — these are context, not the mechanism's core theoretical
grounding.

**Note on naming**: the official academic paper describes the
Shapley-value-based ranking and trust-weighted consensus mechanism but does
not use the name "Yuma Consensus" anywhere in that document. "Yuma
Consensus" as a named, specific algorithm (stake-weighted median + outlier
clipping) appears in community/ecosystem documentation and later working
papers rather than in the cited academic source itself — flagged here as a
naming gap between the academic grounding and the term actually used in
practice.

Known limitations.markdown:
- **Weight copying**: validators can copy other validators' submitted
  weights to earn rewards without doing the underlying evaluation work,
  free-riding on honest validators. Acknowledged as a known issue — a
  working paper titled *"Weight Copying in Bittensor"* (Opentensor, May
  2024) exists specifically addressing it, though the document's full
  content could not be retrieved directly for this entry (link redirected
  to a generic docs page: https://docs.learnbittensor.org/papers/BT_Weight_Copier-29May2024.pdf).
  Flagged as inferred-exists, content-unverified.
- **Governance centralization tension**: validator/stake concentration has
  drawn scrutiny over how decentralized the network actually is in
  practice. [Yellow.com research](https://yellow.com/research/bittensor-decentralized-ai-market-control-2026)
  raises this; not independently verified here.
- **Naming/documentation gap**: as noted above, the specific "Yuma
  Consensus" algorithm described in secondary sources isn't the same
  document as the academic paper citing Shapley values — the primary
  academic source and the commonly-cited mechanism name don't fully line up,
  which makes precise grounding harder than for the other tracked systems.

What it does.markdown:
EZKL (zkonduit/ezkl) compiles ONNX-format ML models (exported from
PyTorch, TensorFlow, sklearn, etc.) into a zero-knowledge circuit, so
that a model inference can be proven correct without revealing the
model weights and/or inputs, and verified cheaply — including on-chain
in the EVM, in a browser, or on-device.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- Takes an ONNX graph + sample input, compiles a corresponding proving
  circuit, generates a proof of correct execution, and a matching
  verifier (including Solidity verifier contracts for EVM chains).
- Backend proving system: **Halo2**. EZKL's own README states: "In the
  backend we use the collaboratively-developed
  [Halo2](https://github.com/privacy-scaling-explorations/halo2) as a
  proof system." ([github.com/zkonduit/ezkl](https://github.com/zkonduit/ezkl))
- EZKL uses a modified variant of Halo2 that swaps in **KZG polynomial
  commitments** (rather than the discrete-log/IPA commitment Halo2
  originally shipped with) specifically to get smaller proofs and
  cheaper on-chain verification. This is a deliberate deviation from
  vanilla Halo2, not an assumption — flagged as inferred-from-general
  sourcing rather than a single explicit EZKL doc quote; worth
  rechecking against current docs.ezkl.xyz if this matters for a
  specific decision.

**Two-hop grounding, not a direct citation** — EZKL's own docs don't
cite an academic paper directly. The chain is:

1. EZKL's README/docs explicitly name **Halo2**
   ([privacy-scaling-explorations/halo2](https://github.com/privacy-scaling-explorations/halo2))
   as the proof system it uses.
2. Halo2's own design book explicitly states: *"The arithmetization
   used by Halo 2 comes from [PLONK](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/953),
   or more precisely its extension UltraPLONK that supports custom
   gates and lookup arguments."*
   ([zcash.github.io/halo2/concepts/arithmetization.html](https://zcash.github.io/halo2/concepts/arithmetization.html))

So: EZKL → (names) Halo2 → (cites) PLONK paper. See
`/foundations/zkml.md` for the paper itself. Halo2 does **not**, per
its own arithmetization page, discuss the original "Halo" recursive-
proof-composition paper (Bowe/Grigg/Hopwood 2019) — that lineage looked
plausible going in but didn't hold up under direct source-checking, so
it's dropped rather than asserted.

Known limitations.markdown:
- SRS/setup size scales with circuit complexity and can become a real
  deployment cost for larger models.
- Relies on a trusted-setup ceremony for KZG (weaker trust assumption
  than a fully transparent setup) — this is a direct consequence of
  choosing KZG over Halo2's original commitment scheme.
- This entry did not independently verify audit status, current proof
  latency numbers, or maximum practical model size — flag these as
  open follow-ups rather than treating the matrix as complete.

What it does.markdown:
Gensyn is a protocol for decentralized ML compute: clients submit training
jobs, untrusted third-party providers execute them, and a verification layer
lets the client trust the result without controlling or re-running all of the
provider's hardware.

Architecture summary.markdown:
Current production system is **Verde** (per Gensyn's own research blog,
Oct 2026 check), which replaced the older litepaper-era design built around
four roles (Submitters, Solvers, Verifiers, Whistleblowers) and a Truebit-style
challenge game. Verde combines two pieces:

- **RepOps (Reproducible Operators)**: forces a fixed operation ordering for
  ML operators so that execution is bitwise-reproducible across different
  hardware, closing the floating-point non-associativity gap that previously
  made exact-match verification unreliable across GPUs/vendors.
- **Two-level bisection game**: providers commit to each training iteration
  via Merkle trees; disputes are resolved by bisecting first at the iteration
  level, then the operation level, so a referee only has to re-check a small,
  pinpointed slice of the computation instead of re-running the whole job.

Source: [Verde: Verification System In Production](https://www.gensyn.ai/research/verde-verification-system-in-production)
(Gensyn's own research blog).

Note: the older litepaper (docs.gensyn.ai/litepaper) describes a different,
earlier design — a Truebit-style incentive game with Submitter/Solver/
Verifier/Whistleblower roles and a graph-based "pinpoint protocol." That
litepaper is confirmed by Gensyn's own ecosystem write-ups to be **outdated**
relative to Verde. Documented here for lineage, not as current architecture.

What it does.markdown:
Nillion is a decentralized network for storing and computing on encrypted
("blind") data without ever reconstructing the plaintext on any single
node. Data is split and distributed across independent nodes; computation
happens directly on the shares via secure multi-party computation (MPC),
and only the final result is reassembled.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- **Nil Message Compute (NMC)** is Nillion's branding for its MPC layer.
  It combines **One-Time Masking (OTM)** with **Linear Secret Sharing
  (LSS)** so that a network of nodes can jointly store and process
  confidential data with information-theoretic security (unconditionally
  secure, not just computationally hard to break).
- The production MPC protocol built on top of this is internally called
  **Curl**, extended from LSSS to efficiently support non-linear
  operations (division, square roots, trig, logs) that plain linear
  secret sharing can't do without extra machinery.
- In 2026 Nillion migrated its base chain from Cosmos to Ethereum,
  launching a new L1 called **Blacklight** (mainnet live 2026-10-05).
  Node operators stake NIL (minimum 70,000 NIL) to run nodes and verify
  computations. The original Cosmos-based L2 is being wound down, with
  users told to bridge assets to the new L1.

Built on (foundational lineage).markdown:
**Paper:** "Evaluation of Arithmetic Sum-of-Products Expressions in
Linear Secret Sharing Schemes with a Non-Interactive Computation Phase"
— Miguel de Vega (Nillion), Andrei Lapets (Reity), Stanisław Jarecki
(UC Irvine), Wicher Malten (Nillion), Mehmet Ugurbil (Nillion), Wyatt
Howe (UCLA).
PDF: https://nillion.pub/sum-of-products-lsss-non-interactive.pdf
(originally posted to IACR ePrint as 2023/1740, later withdrawn from
ePrint but mirrored on Nillion's own site).

**Grounding source:** Nillion's own team announced this paper directly
as the basis for their non-interactive MPC protocol for non-linear
computation — see "Introducing the Nillion Non-Interactive MPC Protocol
for Non-Linear Computations"
(https://medium.com/@Nillion_Network/introducing-the-nillion-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations-67e9310ef479)
and the MPC Alliance's coverage of the same announcement
(https://www.mpcalliance.org/blog/nillion-introduces-a-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations).
Four of the six authors are Nillion staff, so this is effectively
Nillion publishing its own core protocol paper — about as direct a
grounding as this kind of claim can get.

**How it's used:** the paper's contribution — evaluating arithmetic
sum-of-products expressions (which covers the multiplications needed
for non-linear ops) within LSSS using a preprocessing phase instead of
interactive communication during computation — is the specific technique
that lets Curl/NMC do non-linear math without the usual back-and-forth
communication overhead of classic MPC protocols.

Known limitations.markdown:
- The specific foundational paper above was **withdrawn from IACR ePrint**
  (official listing shows 2023/1740 withdrawn 2024-06-28); the only
  available copy is now self-hosted by Nillion at nillion.pub. Worth
  tracking why it was withdrawn — could be a correction, a priority
  dispute, or something more substantive. Flagged here as an open
  question rather than resolved.
- Nillion markets both MPC and homomorphic-encryption-style techniques
  under the "blind computation" umbrella; some public-facing material
  blurs which specific guarantee (information-theoretic MPC vs.
  computationally-secure HE) applies to which product surface. Treat
  marketing claims about "which crypto is doing the work" with caution
  until cross-checked against the underlying protocol docs.
- Mid-2026 chain migration (Cosmos → Ethereum L1) and L2 shutdown is
  recent and operationally disruptive — a useful thing to watch for
  whether it introduces new trust assumptions (e.g. bridge security)
  not present in the original MPC design.

What it does.markdown:
Concrete-ML is an open-source Python framework from Zama that lets you train
a model normally (scikit-learn-compatible APIs, or PyTorch/TensorFlow via
ONNX) and then run inference on **encrypted** inputs, so the service running
the model never sees the plaintext data. Output of `encrypt()` → `run()` →
`decrypt()` never exposes intermediate values to the server.

Architecture summary.markdown:
- Built directly on top of **Concrete** (Zama's TFHE compiler, which turns
  Python/numerical programs into their FHE equivalent), which itself is
  built on **TFHE-rs**, Zama's Rust implementation of the TFHE scheme.
- Models are **quantized** (quantization-aware training or post-training
  quantization) to convert floating-point weights/activations into
  integers, since FHE arithmetic operates over integers, not floats.
- Non-linear activation functions (ReLU, sigmoid, etc.) are evaluated via
  **programmable bootstrapping** — TFHE's bootstrap step is repurposed to

Known limitations.markdown:
- Bootstrapping is the dominant cost; deeper/wider networks with more
  non-linearities scale poorly in latency compared to plaintext inference.
- Quantization-aware training adds workflow overhead and can cost accuracy
  versus the unquantized model.
- Encrypted inference latency (seconds–minutes per call depending on model
  size) remains far from plaintext inference speed — not yet suited to
  low-latency, high-throughput serving.

frontmatter.field: Decentralized incentive / consensus mechanisms for ML networks
frontmatter.venue: Contributions to the Theory of Games, Vol. II (Annals of Mathematics Studies 28), Princeton University Press

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Bittensor's own academic paper, *"Incentivizing Intelligence: The Bittensor
Approach"* (Steeves et al., hosted at
[bittensor.com/academia](https://www.bittensor.com/academia)), explicitly
cites Shapley's 1952 value concept as the theoretical basis for how the
network attributes credit to peers: each participant's reward is meant to
reflect their marginal contribution to the network's informational output,
evaluated across permutations of coalitions of peers — which is exactly what
the Shapley value formalizes. This is the one piece of the Bittensor stack
with a clean, explicit academic citation; the rest of the mechanism (the
specific stake-weighted-median "Yuma Consensus" algorithm used in
production) is documented in community/ecosystem sources rather than in a
peer-reviewed citation trail — see the naming-gap note in
[[systems/bittensor]].

Core contribution.markdown:
Shapley's paper answers a fairness question: if a group of people (or
agents) jointly produce some value by cooperating, how should that value be
split among them in a way that fairly reflects each one's contribution,
even when contributions aren't independent (i.e. what one agent adds
depends on who else is already in the group)? The Shapley value is defined
by averaging each agent's marginal contribution across every possible order
in which agents could join the coalition. It's the unique allocation rule
satisfying a small set of fairness axioms (efficiency, symmetry, additivity,
null-player). It's a cooperative-game-theory result, not a machine-learning
or cryptography result — its relevance here is purely as the attribution
principle a decentralized ML incentive system borrows.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Bittensor needs to answer: "how much is this peer's model output actually
worth to the network, given that other peers are also contributing similar
or overlapping information?" Naively rewarding every peer independently
invites redundant, low-effort submissions; the Shapley framing is invoked to
justify rewarding marginal/novel contribution instead. In practice,
production Bittensor does not compute literal Shapley values (that's
computationally intractable at network scale — exact Shapley values require
summing over all coalition permutations); it uses Yuma Consensus's
stake-weighted-median-with-clipping as a tractable proxy mechanism inspired
by the same fairness goal. This is worth flagging explicitly: the citation
grounds the *motivation*, not the *literal algorithm* actually running in
production.

frontmatter.authors: Hengrui Jia, Mohammad Yaghini, Christopher A. Choquette-Choo, Natalie Dullerud, Anvith Thudi, Varun Chandrasekaran, Nicolas Papernot
frontmatter.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2021

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Cited directly by Gensyn's own Verde research post as foundational prior work
("Proof-of-Learning" — [arxiv.org/abs/2103.05633](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.05633)),
alongside Refereed Delegation, Agatha, Toploc, and Proof-of-Training-Data. See
[systems/gensyn.md](../systems/gensyn.md) for the full citation list and source
link. Of that list, this paper is the one that directly frames the core problem
Gensyn's verification layer exists to solve: how do you let a party that didn't
do the training convince a verifier that specific gradient-descent work was
actually performed, without full re-execution.

Core contribution.markdown:
Introduces "proof-of-learning" (PoL): a party that trained a model produces a
proof — built from checkpoints and the gradient-descent trajectory metadata
recorded during training — that lets a verifier check, cheaply, that training
actually happened as claimed, rather than requiring the verifier to redo the
entire training run. It formalizes what such a proof needs to guarantee and
shows practical constructions and attacks against naive versions of the idea.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Gensyn's verification problem is exactly this: a client needs to trust that a
third-party provider trained a model correctly without re-running the full
job. Gensyn's current production system (Verde) does not implement PoL's
checkpoint-trajectory scheme directly — it instead uses RepOps
(bitwise-reproducible operators) plus a Merkle-tree-based bisection/dispute
game — but PoL is the paper that established the problem framing and the
first concrete proposal in this space, which is why Gensyn cites it as prior
work. See [systems/gensyn.md](../systems/gensyn.md) for how the current
architecture actually differs from PoL's approach.

frontmatter.paper: Deep Neural Networks for Encrypted Inference with TFHE
frontmatter.authors: Andrei Stoian, Jordan Frery, Roman Bredehoft, Luis Montero, Celia Kherfallah, Benoit Chevallier-Mames

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Authored by the team behind Zama's Concrete-ML, and uses Concrete directly
for its benchmarks — this is the paper that connects the general TFHE
cryptosystem to the specific problem of running deep neural network
inference on encrypted data, which is exactly what Concrete-ML ships as a
product. It sits one layer above the raw cryptography (TFHE itself, and
Chillotti/Joye/Paillier's programmable bootstrapping) and one layer below
the shipped library — the applied bridge.

Core contribution.markdown:
The paper shows how to design and quantize DNN architectures (targeted at
computer-vision tasks) so that they can run entirely under TFHE's
programmable bootstrapping, and benchmarks the resulting latency/accuracy
tradeoffs on Concrete. The core insight it operationalizes: FHE arithmetic
only works cleanly over integers, so every layer of the network has to be
re-expressed in quantized integer form *before* bootstrapping is used to
evaluate non-linearities — the paper is effectively the recipe for doing
that re-expression without destroying accuracy or blowing up latency.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
Concrete-ML's quantization-aware training pipeline and its approach to
evaluating activation functions via programmable bootstrapping are the
productionized version of what this paper demonstrates. See
`/systems/zama-concrete-ml.md` for the property matrix this paper's
techniques feed into — specifically the "Precision" and "Non-linear
evaluation" rows.

frontmatter.paper: Evaluation of Arithmetic Sum-of-Products Expressions in Linear Secret Sharing Schemes with a Non-Interactive Computation Phase
frontmatter.authors: Miguel de Vega, Andrei Lapets, Stanisław Jarecki, Wicher Malten, Mehmet Ugurbil, Wyatt Howe
frontmatter.venue: self-published / IACR ePrint 2023/1740 (withdrawn 2024-06-28; mirrored at nillion.pub)

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Nillion's own team announced this paper as the direct basis for their
non-interactive MPC protocol for non-linear computation — see
"Introducing the Nillion Non-Interactive MPC Protocol for Non-Linear
Computations"
(https://medium.com/@Nillion_Network/introducing-the-nillion-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations-67e9310ef479),
corroborated by the MPC Alliance's write-up of the same announcement
(https://www.mpcalliance.org/blog/nillion-introduces-a-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations).
Four of the six listed authors (de Vega, Malten, Ugurbil, and one more)
are Nillion staff — this is effectively the project publishing its own
core protocol paper, which is about the strongest grounding available
for a "foundational paper" claim in this exercise.

Core contribution.markdown:
Classic linear secret sharing schemes (LSSS) handle addition of shared
secrets for free but need rounds of communication between parties to
handle multiplication — the operation needed for anything non-linear.
This paper describes a way to evaluate arithmetic sum-of-products
expressions (sums of products of shared values — covers the multiply
step) using a **preprocessing phase that doesn't depend on the private
inputs**, so the actual computation-on-private-data step becomes
non-interactive. In plain terms: move the expensive "parties have to
talk to each other" part of secure multiplication to a setup phase that
can happen before anyone's real data is involved, so the live computation
is faster and doesn't require synchronous coordination between nodes.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
This is the specific technique underneath Nillion's **Curl** protocol,
which extends LSSS to support the non-linear math (division, square
roots, trig, logarithms) that ML workloads need but plain secret sharing
can't do cheaply. It's the piece that lets Nillion's MPC layer process
more than just linear operations on encrypted data, which is the gap
between "toy secret sharing demo" and "can actually run ML inference
on shared data."

Open question for future monitoring.markdown:
The paper was withdrawn from IACR ePrint (2023/1740, withdrawn
2024-06-28) and now only exists as a Nillion-hosted PDF. No public
explanation found for the withdrawal. If a future paper-watch run
surfaces commentary on *why* it was withdrawn (correction vs. priority
dispute vs. something substantive), that's worth a dedicated note since
it bears directly on how much to trust this as the field's seed paper.

frontmatter.paper: PLONK: Permutations over Lagrange-bases for Oecumenical Noninteractive arguments of Knowledge
frontmatter.authors: Ariel Gabizon, Zachary J. Williamson, Oana Ciobotaru

Why this is the seed for this field.markdown:
Grounded via a two-hop citation chain, not a direct EZKL citation:

- EZKL's own README names **Halo2** as its backend proof system.
- Halo2's own design documentation states explicitly: *"The
  arithmetization used by Halo 2 comes from
  [PLONK](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/953), or more precisely its
  extension UltraPLONK that supports custom gates and lookup
  arguments."*
  ([zcash.github.io/halo2/concepts/arithmetization.html](https://zcash.github.io/halo2/concepts/arithmetization.html))

So the tracked system (EZKL) is built on Halo2, which is explicitly
built on this paper's arithmetization. This is as close to "grounded"
as the chain gets without EZKL citing PLONK by name itself.

Halo2's own design documentation states explicitly: *"The arithmetization used by Halo 2 comes from [PLONK](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/953), or more precisely its extension UltraPLONK that supports custom gates and lookup arguments."* ([zcash.github.io/halo2/concepts/arithmetization.html](https://zcash.github.io/halo2/concepts/arithmetization.html)) So the tracked system (EZKL) is built on Halo2, which is explicitly built on this paper's arithmetization. This is as close to "grounded" as the chain gets without EZKL citing PLONK by name itself.

Core contribution.markdown:
PLONK introduced a practical, universal (not circuit-specific) SNARK
construction: a single structured reference string works for *any*
circuit up to a size bound, instead of needing a fresh trusted setup
per circuit (as earlier SNARKs like the original Groth16/Pinocchio
pipeline required). It does this via a permutation argument over
Lagrange-basis polynomials to enforce wiring constraints between gates,
combined with a polynomial commitment scheme (originally KZG) to make
the whole thing non-interactive and succinct. Follow-on work extended
this base arithmetization with custom gates and lookup arguments
("UltraPLONK" / "PLONKish"), which is the specific extension Halo2
actually implements.

Link to tracked system.markdown:
EZKL inherits PLONKish arithmetization transitively through Halo2, then
additionally swaps Halo2's native commitment scheme for KZG commitments
specifically to shrink proof size and verification cost for on-chain
use (see `/systems/ezkl.md` — this specific claim is flagged inferred,
not directly quoted from an EZKL source, so re-verify before treating
it as settled). The universality property of PLONK (one SRS per size
bound, not per circuit) is part of why a general-purpose tool like
EZKL — which has to support arbitrary ONNX graphs rather than one fixed
circuit — is practical at all.
